newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe horticultural exports growth revised down.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe horticultural exports growth revised down.

text.p: Zimbabwe expects to earn Z$1.5 billion from horticulture exports in the marketing season ending in June, up from Z$997.4 million last year, an industry official said on Tuesday.
But Stanley Heri, chief executive of the Horticultural Promotion Council (HPC), said his organisation had lowered earlier estimates for export growth to 25 percent from 30 percent.
He attributed this to unfavourable weather in Zimbabwe and in its overseas market destinations.

"The volume of cut flowers in Zimbabwe was down because of the continuous overcast weather (between November and February this year)," Heri said. "Our key marketing period coincided with a cold spell in Europe that affected not only our customers but also surface distribution."
But Heri predicted citrus exports would be up on earlier estimates with a growth of 36 percent, with mango fruit enjoying increased demand overseas.
"The market for exotic fruit is very strong. Mangoes are a growing crop with 600 tonnes exported this year, a 50 percent increase on last year," he said.
Airfreighting had maintained "a good standard" with flights going out every day of the week. Some 15 carriers now offer their services, breaking a monopoly formerly held by state carrier Affretair.
Besides Affretair, other carriers include Air Zimbabwe, British Airways, Qantas, TAP, Lufthansa, Air Mauritius, Air France, KLM and South African Airways.
Between July and February, the airfreighters transported over 9,390 tonnes of flowers to overseas destinations while other produce accounted for 5,880 tonnes. Comparative figures are unavailable.

Holland remained Zimbabwe's biggest market for cut flowers at over 74 percent of the market share, largely the same as last season, while most of the fruit and vegetables were bound for Britain, which took in over 54 percent of produce.
Heri said while horticulture continued to be one of the fastest-growing industries, there was increasing competition from Brazil, Colombia, Israel, Kenya, Morocco and Zambia.

"The symptoms from the marketplace for both flowers and vegetables indicate severe competition from our peer countries. This means Zimbabwe has to concentrate on quality...of both product and service," Heri said.
